headline: Massachusetts awards $330M for housing and local growth projects
dek: The largest Community One Stop for Growth round to date is expected to support more than 27,000 homes and 13,000 permanent jobs, with South Coast communities receiving $6.5 million for housing, infrastructure and downtown reuse.
body: Massachusetts is directing $330 million to 403 housing and economic-development projects in 207 communities, the Healey administration announced Oct. 1. State officials say the fiscal 2027 Community One Stop for Growth awards are the largest single round in the program's history and are expected to support more than 27,000 new homes, more than 13,000 permanent jobs and more than 7 million square feet of commercial development. The administration also estimates that the projects could help unlock $24.6 billion in private investment. Those are projected results, not homes or jobs already delivered.

The awards are designed to help cities, towns and other organizations move projects from planning to construction or reuse. The state describes the Community One Stop for Growth as a coordinated application and review process for housing and economic-development programs, rather than a single construction grant. The current awards are being administered through 14 programs involving the Executive Office of Economic Development, the Executive Office of Housing and Livable Communities, and MassDevelopment, according to the Massachusetts Municipal Association's account of the announcement. The state's program overview is available at https://www.mass.gov/info-details/community-one-stop-for-growth.

The largest portions of the round are aimed at infrastructure that can make development possible. The Massachusetts Municipal Association reported $109.7 million for 54 HousingWorks Infrastructure projects, $105.1 million for 59 MassWorks projects and $51.1 million for 24 MBTA Community Catalyst Fund projects. Other awards cover underused properties, seaport-related work, rural development, downtown improvements, site readiness, planning and brownfield redevelopment. The mix matters because a housing proposal can stall for reasons that are not solved by building financing alone, including streets, utilities, site cleanup and public-space improvements.

The geographic reach is also part of the administration's case for the program. The awards extend to every region of Massachusetts, and the municipal association said 13 communities are receiving One Stop funding for the first time. The administration's breakdown, as reported by the association, puts 36% of projects in rural communities, 24% in Gateway Cities, 37% in Housing Choice Communities and about half in MBTA Communities. That distribution describes the locations of awarded projects; it does not guarantee that each community will produce the number of homes or jobs projected for the statewide round.

On the South Coast, New Bedford-area communities are set to receive $6.5 million, according to New Bedford Guide. New Bedford's share totals $4,079,800, including $600,000 for repairs and life-safety upgrades at the Star Store in the downtown arts district. The work is intended to help artists and creative developers reoccupy the building as it moves toward a planned 2027 reopening. Another $900,000 will support the conversion of a vacant former nursing home on Acushnet Avenue into dozens of workforce-housing units, while other awards address riverside development, waterfront and downtown lighting, and public-safety infrastructure. The local report is at https://www.newbedfordguide.com/6-5-million-awarded-economic-development-grants-new-bedford-senate-district/2026/10/01.

Dartmouth is slated to receive $2.265 million, most of it for sewer-pump improvements and replacements intended to add capacity for new housing, New Bedford Guide reported. A smaller Dartmouth award will study potential uses for a former police station. Fairhaven will use funding for improvements around the Pease Park boating area, including stormwater work and public amenities, while Mattapoisett will develop standards for its Village Business District. Those local examples show how the statewide program combines housing production with the less visible infrastructure and planning work that supports it.

The Massachusetts Municipal Association, which represents the state's cities and towns, said local governments often lack the resources to take on projects of this scale without state partnerships. That is an advocacy group's assessment, not an independent evaluation of the awards' economic return. For residents, the practical test will be whether the money leads to completed infrastructure, occupied homes, reopened commercial space and sustained employment rather than remaining at the announcement stage.

The state says the full list of recipients and project descriptions is available through its Community One Stop for Growth awards dashboard at https://www.mass.gov/info-details/community-one-stop-for-growth-awards. The program schedule says contracting is expected to begin in November 2026. Project timing will vary by municipality and grant program, so the next milestones are contracting, local approvals and construction or reuse work. The Oct. 1 announcement establishes the awards and their projected benefits; later records will show which projects advance and which targets are ultimately met.
author: NorthEast News Desk
